content.text: {"persuasion":"PERSUADED","support_scope":"FULL","rationale":"The book's entry defines belief as receiving God's testimony as governing truth in a response that submits to it, distinguishes this from the bare assent even demons possess, and reads persistent disobedience as the exposure of unbelief. Every clause of that printed entry is carried directly by the cited texts. John 3:36 in the Greek contrasts ho pisteuon (the one believing) with ho apeithon (the one disobeying), making disobedience the stated antonym of belief in the verse most often quoted for belief-as-trust. Romans 10:16 interchanges 'obeyed the gospel' with Isaiah's 'who hath believed our report,' treating the two verbs as one covenant response. Hebrews 3:18-19 does the same in reverse: the wilderness generation's exclusion is attributed in v.18 to those who were disobedient (apeithesasin, KJV 'believed not') and in v.19 to apistia, 'unbelief' — the very equation the book asserts. James 2:19-22 supplies the entry's foil (demonic assent that is real but not saving) and its positive case (Abraham's belief brought to its declared end by obedient works). John 12:42-43 and Mark 1:27 supply human and demonic examples of genuine fact-acceptance overridden by a rival governing love or reduced to compelled compliance, which the entry explicitly accommodates rather than denies. The strongest counter-reading — classical Protestant fiducia, in which belief is inward trust and obedience is only its inevitable fruit — identifies the same referent (saving trust in Christ beyond assent, necessarily issuing in obedience) and so does not contradict the book's core; it disputes only whether submission is constitutive of belief or consequent upon it, a mechanism dispute. It also explains the belief/disobedience lexical interchange in John 3:36, Rom 10:16, and Heb 3:18 less directly, requiring an inferential step (obedience as evidence) where the book reads the texts' own vocabulary at face value. No supplied text is explained by the counter that the book's identification cannot explain. The entry is also careful not to overreach: it states that belief is 'not obedience renamed,' preserving the assent/trust component the common interpretation insists on. On inference to best explanation across the actual cited evidence, the book wins.","book_core_identification":"To believe, in the saving sense, is to receive God's testimony as governing truth in a response that submits to it — such that belief and obedience are two faces of one covenant response, and persistent refusal to obey is what Scripture itself calls unbelief. This is distinct from bare assent (which demons share) and is not reducible to a private inner state that asks nothing of conduct.","book_secondary_elaborations":["Scripture also uses 'believe' for mere fact-acceptance (demons in Jas 2:19; rulers in John 12:42-43), a real but non-saving belief overridden by a rival governing love or fear.","Belief holds a distinct office among four converging covenant words (love = the keeping, knowing = the covenant bond, faith = trust held steady in hope, belief = receiving the word as governing truth).","Abraham's offering of Isaac did not replace his belief but brought it to its declared end, 'by works was faith made perfect' (Jas 2:21-22).","The KJV's rendering of apeitheo as 'believe not' in several places reflects the translators' own recognition of the belief/obedience overlap.","Demonic compliance under command (Mark 1:27) illustrates assent plus compelled obedience that is still not covenant allegiance."],"strongest_counter_interpretation":"The classical Protestant (sola fide) reading: saving belief is fiducia — personal trust in and reliance upon Christ, composed of knowledge, assent, and heart-trust — which is itself purely receptive of grace. Obedience and works are the necessary and inevitable fruit and evidence of genuine belief, but are not part of belief's definition. On this reading John 3:36 and Heb 3:18-19 pair unbelief with disobedience because disobedience is the outward evidence of absent trust, not because submission is internal to the act of believing; Rom 10:16 uses 'obeyed the gospel' as shorthand for the obedience of responding to the gospel's summons to trust; James 2 teaches that dead faith is exposed by its lack of fruit, not that works enter faith's essence.","counter_core_identification":"Belief is inward personal trust in and reliance upon Christ for salvation (notitia, assensus, fiducia); obedience necessarily follows from it as fruit and evidence but is not constitutive of it.","counter_relation_to_book_core":"SAME_CORE_BROADER","material_core_denial":"There is no material core denial. Both readings identify the same referent: a saving response to God's testimony about Christ that exceeds intellectual assent, that even the demons' real assent does not attain, and whose absence is reliably exposed by persistent disobedience. The counter disputes only the mechanism — whether the submitting response is internal to belief or its inevitable consequence — and both positions predict the same textual pattern of belief and obedience standing or falling together.","counter_case":["Fiducia preserves the purely receptive character of faith demanded by Eph 2:8-9 and Rom 4:5 ('to him that worketh not, but believeth'), keeping justification free of works as ground.","Apeitheo can be glossed 'refuse to be persuaded,' allowing John 3:36 and Heb 3:18 to describe unbelief's root (unpersuadedness) rather than defining belief as submission.","James 2 can be read as concerning the demonstration of faith before men ('shew me thy faith'), so dead faith is spurious faith, not faith lacking an obedience-component.","John 12:42-43 shows 'believed' used of an inner conviction withheld from public expression, suggesting belief per se is an inner state and confession/obedience is a separable act.","Rom 10:9-10, in the same chapter as 10:16, defines the saving response as heart-belief plus confession, which fits trust-plus-fruit as naturally as trust-as-submission."],"book_explanatory_advantages":["John 3:36 is explained at face value: the text's own antonym for 'believeth on the Son' is 'obeyeth not the Son' (apeithon), which the book's definition predicts and the fiducia reading must mediate through an extra evidential step.","Heb 3:18-19's tight interchange — 'them that believed not' (Greek: were disobedient) / 'could not enter in because of unbelief' — is exactly the equation the book asserts: the refusal that exposed distrust was disobedience.","Rom 10:16's parallelism ('not all obeyed the gospel... who hath believed our report?') treats obeying and believing as one response to one message, which the book's definition renders without remainder.","The book cleanly stratifies the counter-evidence: demonic assent (Jas 2:19, real belief, real trembling, no allegiance), compelled compliance (Mark 1:27, obedience without covenant), and suppressed conviction (John 12:42-43, fact-belief governed by a rival love) are each placed without strain, showing why Scripture can call all of these 'believe' while denying they save.","The Abraham case (Jas 2:21-22) is explained as belief perfected — brought to its end — by works, matching James's own verb ('by works was faith made perfect') rather than treating works as mere external certification.","The definition explicitly avoids the overcorrection ('not obedience renamed'), so it does not collapse into works-righteousness and remains consistent with the assent/trust texts the common interpretation cites."],"counter_explanatory_advantages":["It integrates more smoothly with the wider Pauline receptive-faith texts (Rom 4:5, Eph 2:8-9) that are not in this entry's citation list but shape the common interpretation.","It offers a low-cost account of John 12:42-43 in which 'believed' straightforwardly denotes an inner state that failed to issue in confession.","It preserves a sharp category distinction between the ground of justification (trust) and its evidence (works), guarding against reading James 2:21 as works
